questions.topic: Status of the Guide vs FDA
questions.question: How does the FDA endorsement letter (2000) describe the regulatory status of the ISPE Baseline Guide?

options.A: The guide was developed and is owned solely by ISPE and is not an FDA regulation or guidance; building to it does not guarantee compliance with FDA requirements
options.B: The guide has been formally adopted by the FDA as a guidance document, and systems built to it are regarded as complying with cGMP requirements and exempt from inspection
options.C: The content of the guide was reviewed and approved chapter by chapter by the FDA and became the official implementing rules of 21 CFR 211
options.D: The guide is a standard jointly owned by the FDA and ISPE, with only the appendices being non-mandatory

questions.explanation: The letter states explicitly that the Guide was created and is owned solely by ISPE and is not an FDA regulation, standard or guidance, and that conforming to it does not mean automatic compliance with FDA requirements. The FDA merely offered comments for ISPE's consideration, and the appendices were not reviewed by the FDA at all.

questions.question: How does this guide treat validation (commissioning and qualification) of water and steam systems?

options.A: It does not discuss it in depth, as it is covered by the Commissioning and Qualification Baseline Guide
options.B: It devotes a chapter to fully specifying all IQ/OQ/PQ test items, acceptance criteria and document templates
options.C: It does not mention it at all, because validation is the FDA's responsibility and not an engineering matter, so industry need not deal with it or document it
options.D: It specifies validation of water systems only, with validation of steam systems governed separately by USP and ASME

questions.explanation: Section 1.2 states that the guide focuses on engineering issues in the design, construction and operation of new systems and is not a detailed design guide; validation is not discussed in depth here but is left to the C&Q Baseline Guide.

questions.question: According to Section 1.4, in a new pharmaceutical water or steam system, what is the most critical step from regulatory, technical and financial perspectives?

options.A: Selecting the final treatment technology (such as distillation or RO), because equipment price makes up the bulk of total cost
options.B: Deciding the storage tank material and surface finish, because this directly determines microbiological quality
options.C: Completing the IQ/OQ/PQ validation plan, because validation cost exceeds equipment cost
options.D: Setting the specification for the required water or steam quality, because it has the greatest effect on lifecycle cost

questions.explanation: Once set, the specification affects lifecycle cost more than any later design decision, so designers should consult the quality unit and technical experts early. Technology and material choices are dealt with only after the specification.

questions.topic: Critical process parameters for microbial control
questions.question: The microbial quality of a water system cannot be monitored in real time. According to the guide's concept of critical parameters, which is most likely to be regarded as a critical parameter?

options.A: Parameters that control microbial growth, such as circulation temperature, UV intensity or ozone concentration
options.B: The supply pressure of the steam boiler, because it affects steam consumption and boiler operating efficiency
options.C: The insulation thickness of the storage tank shell, because it affects heat loss and system energy consumption
options.D: The operators' shift schedule, because it affects sampling frequency and personnel training hours

questions.explanation: A critical parameter is one that directly affects product quality. Microbial quality cannot be monitored directly in real time, so reliance is placed on parameters that control microbial growth (temperature, UV intensity, ozone concentration, circulation, etc.); chemical purity, by contrast, can be monitored directly as a quality attribute at each step.

questions.question: According to the explanation of Good Engineering Practice (GEP) in Section 1.4, what does GEP recommend manufacturers do?

options.A: Treat all systems uniformly by GMP validation, without distinguishing critical from non-critical, for consistency
options.B: Complete commissioning first and then invite QA to review, to avoid interfering with engineering progress and construction schedules
options.C: Create independent documents for each stage, so that execution of each stage can be audited separately later
options.D: Involve stakeholders such as engineering, operations and QA early, so that the system needs to be documented only once

questions.explanation: GEP holds that all systems, including water systems, need some form of commissioning/qualification, with documentation, inspection and field testing; involving all parties early lets the system be "documented only once", reducing duplicated work.

questions.question: According to the USP monographs, which of the following explicit requirements does Water for Injection have in addition to Purified Water?

options.A: The source water must comply with the EPA National Primary Drinking Water Regulations and be tested batch by batch (Purified Water has no such requirement)
options.B: It must meet conductivity requirements and a pH range (not required for Purified Water)
options.C: It must contain no added substances, including pretreatment chemicals (Purified Water allows small amounts of added substances)
options.D: It must meet the bacterial endotoxin test (≤ 0.25 EU/mL) and be finally purified by distillation or RO

questions.explanation: WFI must meet all of the requirements of Purified Water, plus the endotoxin limit and final purification by distillation or RO. Drinking water as source water, conductivity, TOC and "no added substances" are requirements common to both, so these three are not additional for WFI.

questions.question: USP replaced the former USP 22 wet-chemical "oxidizable substances" test with a TOC test. What TOC limit was set?

options.A: 0.05 ppm (50 ppb)
options.B: 0.5 ppm (500 ppb)
options.C: 5 ppm (5,000 ppb)
options.D: 0.1 ppm (100 ppb)

questions.explanation: Based on studies and industry surveys, USP set the TOC limit at 0.5 ppm (500 ppb). 0.05 mg/L is the instrument limit of detection requirement and not a water quality limit, which is easily confused.

questions.question: A plant wants to produce compendial WFI directly with an ultrafiltration (UF) system, since UF has been shown to produce water meeting the endotoxin limit. According to the guide, which judgment is correct?

options.A: Not allowed; although UF water quality is good, regulations do not permit it for producing compendial WFI, and only distillation and RO are accepted
options.B: Allowed, as long as endotoxin and TOC both meet the WFI specification, with no restriction on process method and no need for separate confirmation from the regulatory authority
options.C: Allowed, but a DI and a 0.2 μm filtration must be added after the UF as the final treatment steps
options.D: Not allowed, because the endotoxin removal capability of UF is insufficient to reach the 0.25 EU/mL limit

questions.explanation: The guide states that UF has been used successfully to produce water with strict endotoxin limits but, by regulation, cannot be used to produce compendial-grade WFI; USP accepts only distillation and one other technology, RO. The problem lies not in removal capability but in the regulatory acceptance of the method.

questions.topic: Design, Allowable and Normal Operating Range
questions.question: A system has a Design Condition of 0.5 μS/cm conductivity, an Allowable Operating Range of 1.3 μS/cm or better, and the manufacturer has set a Normal Operating Range of about 1.0 μS/cm or better. The reading during operation is 1.2 μS/cm. Which statement is correct?

options.A: It exceeds the design condition of 0.5 μS/cm, so the system is unacceptable from a cGMP standpoint and must be taken out of service immediately
options.B: It exceeds the Normal Operating Range, which is regarded as a deviation from validated parameters and must be entered in the batch record
options.C: Because it is below 1.3 μS/cm it is still within the Normal Operating Range, and no action is needed
options.D: It is still within the Allowable Operating Range and acceptable from a cGMP standpoint, but it is outside the Normal Operating Range

questions.explanation: Acceptability from a cGMP standpoint depends on being within the Allowable Operating Range; the Normal Operating Range must lie within the Allowable range and is set by the manufacturer for comfortable operation. What must be entered in the batch record is an Action Limit excursion.

questions.question: The guide recommends that manufacturers use Alert and Action limits together with the Normal Operating Range. What is the difference between them?

options.A: The Alert limit is set from operating experience, with corrective action started before the Action limit is reached; the Action limit is based on acceptance criteria, and excursions must be entered in the batch record
options.B: The Alert limit is determined by product acceptance criteria, and excursions must be entered in the batch record; the Action limit is set from operating experience and used for trend management and early warning
options.C: Both have values specified by USP, which the manufacturer may not adjust, nor set stricter internal limits or trend management criteria
options.D: Alert limit excursions must be entered in the batch record; the Action limit is for engineering reference only and requires no corrective action

questions.explanation: The Alert limit is an early warning that lets you act before crossing the line; the Action limit indicates a deviation from validated parameters and must be entered in the batch record. The order and basis cannot be reversed.

questions.question: According to Chapter 3, how is "suitable non-compendial process water" defined?

options.A: It must meet all of the specifications and tests of Purified Water, and is simply not listed in a USP monograph
options.B: It may be water from any source, without first meeting drinking water requirements, as long as microbiological requirements are met and QA approves
options.C: It meets drinking water requirements and is then given additional treatment to satisfy the process; it need not meet USP water specifications and is often named after the final treatment step
options.D: Its quality is necessarily lower than compendial water, so its production and qualification costs are also lower, and no validation is needed

questions.explanation: Non-compendial water starts from drinking water plus the treatment the process requires, and the manufacturer can set suitable quality and test standards for the product. It is not necessarily lower in quality or cheaper than compendial water, and may even be more highly purified.

questions.topic: Decision tree and drug application commitments
questions.question: A plant uses the Figure 3-1 decision tree to determine that a process can use non-compendial water, but its drug application commits to using Purified Water. How should this be handled?

options.A: Follow the decision tree, because it is QA-approved and newer and is sufficient to replace the application commitment
options.B: Take whichever is less costly, supplemented in change control and then implemented
options.C: Switch to WFI, because WFI will certainly satisfy both and the regulatory authority need not be notified
options.D: Follow the commitment in the application, because application commitments take precedence over the decision tree's suggestions

questions.explanation: The decision tree note states explicitly that "Commitments made in drug applications override suggestions of this decision tree". The decision tree needs supporting documentation and QA review, but still cannot override the application.

questions.question: In the Use-Point Criteria table, a CIP system and a stopper washer are both used on the same day but not at the same time. How should this be handled when determining the distribution loop pipe size?

options.A: Add the two flows together to ensure there is enough at any time, with an extra safety margin
options.B: Take only the higher of the two flows, since they do not occur simultaneously; this is the Diversity Factor
options.C: Take the average of the two flows to avoid oversizing and lower piping cost, while allowing for simultaneous use
options.D: Provide a separate loop for each, to avoid interference and simplify flow calculation

questions.explanation: Flowrate is mainly used to determine pipe size, while Daily Use affects storage and generation decisions. The Diversity Factor flattens expected usage on the basis that not all loads occur every day or at the same time, so only the higher flow is counted.

questions.question: Section 3.3.2 requires a matrix to be created for each use point. What approach does it recommend when filling in values?

options.A: Record only the maximum flow, leaving other parameters to the later detailed design stage to avoid constraining the design too early
options.B: Set every parameter as a single fixed value so that design conditions are clear and unambiguous, to ease later procurement
options.C: State the pressure, flow and temperature ranges entering the unit, expressed as ranges rather than fixed values, to leave room for optimization
options.D: Record only water grade and purpose, with pressure and temperature decided by the equipment supplier at procurement

questions.explanation: The guide requires the pressure, flow and temperature range to be noted for each use point, and establishing ranges rather than fixed values gives the final design more flexibility and increases opportunities to optimize the system.

questions.question: Comparing central and multiple (distributed) water systems, which statement is consistent with Section 3.4?

options.A: Central has lower initial capital but higher operating and maintenance costs, and needs more standby equipment
options.B: Because each is smaller, multiple systems always have lower total capital and operating costs and are easier to maintain and expand
options.C: There is no cost difference, and the choice depends purely on whether standby equipment and plant space are available
options.D: Central has higher initial capital but lower operating and maintenance costs, and the cost per unit of water may be lower

questions.explanation: The higher capital of a central system is mainly due to larger generation, storage and distribution equipment; multiple systems need less initial investment each, but for the same total capacity capital and operating and maintenance costs may actually be higher.

questions.question: According to Section 4.4, which best describes the issues needing special attention in pretreatment when the final treatment is distillation?

options.A: Suspended solids fouling membranes, requiring SDI to be controlled at 3-5 and prefilter cartridges changed regularly
options.B: Only microorganisms need controlling, since other impurities have little effect on distillation, so pretreatment can be greatly simplified
options.C: Hardness causing scaling and chloride causing corrosion, and distillation cannot tolerate chlorine at all (corrosion and carryover into the product)
options.D: Chlorine and chloramine pass through distillation without effect, so there is no need to remove them in pretreatment

questions.explanation: The concerns for distillation are hardness scaling and chloride corrosion, with no tolerance for chlorine, and some capacity to tolerate particulates. SDI 3-5 and hardness below 1 grain/gallon are targets for membrane systems.

questions.question: Comparing the removal of chlorine and chloramine, which statement is correct?

options.A: Both are adsorbed on activated carbon at comparable rates, so the same contact time and hydraulic velocity can be used
options.B: Chloramine is easier to remove than chlorine, because chloramine does not dissociate and produces no by-products, so contact time can be shortened
options.C: Ammonia can be fully removed by RO and distillation, so it poses no problem and needs no additional monitoring
options.D: Chloramine adsorbs on activated carbon much more slowly, needing longer contact time and lower flow velocity, and may dissociate to ammonium and ammonia

questions.explanation: Chlorine can be removed directly by activated carbon or sulfite; chloramine is more complicated, adsorbs slowly, and may dissociate to ammonium and ammonia. Ammonium can be removed by RO but breaks down to ammonia in distillation, and ammonia can pass through both RO and distillation.

questions.question: According to Section 4.4, if the final treatment is a membrane system, what are the typical control targets for pretreatment?

options.A: SDI below 0.5, and hardness must be zero
options.B: SDI of 3-5, and hardness below 1 grain/gallon
options.C: SDI of 10-15, and hardness below 5 grain/gallon
options.D: Only SDI needs to be controlled; hardness is handled by the membrane itself

questions.explanation: Membrane systems are concerned with fouling by suspended solids and scaling caused when water is removed, so the typical targets are SDI of 3-5 and hardness below 1 grain/gallon.

questions.question: USP requires compendial water to contain "no added substances". What is the guide's position on pretreatment?

options.A: Pretreatment also must never add any chemicals, otherwise it violates USP's no-added-substances requirement
options.B: Any chemicals may be added, as long as the final water passes the conductivity test, with no need to demonstrate removal
options.C: Only chlorine may be added; all other chemicals are prohibited in pretreatment and distribution
options.D: It is not prohibited; as long as the added substances are subsequently removed and do not cause an increase in microorganisms or endotoxin

questions.explanation: The "no added substances" requirement applies to Purified Water and WFI themselves; pretreatment often adds chlorine, acid, sulfite, antiscalants, pH adjusters and so on, which are later removed in pretreatment or final treatment. It is a problem only if they cause microbial growth or increased endotoxin.

questions.question: A plant is considering placing the softener after chlorine removal to extend resin life. According to Section 4.6, what does this choice need to balance?

options.A: Poorer resin life, but because no sanitization is needed, maintenance cost and downtime are lower
options.B: Microbiological problems can be avoided entirely, because a softener treats only minerals and does not affect the microbial and endotoxin load in the water
options.C: Better resin life and capacity, but loss of chlorine protection, requiring periodic hot or chemical sanitization to control microorganisms and endotoxin
options.D: Chlorine below 1 ppm will always damage the resin immediately, so the softener should not be placed before chlorine removal, to avoid shortening its life

questions.explanation: A softener placed before removal of the microbial control agent is protected by chlorine from microbial growth, and chlorine below 1 ppm generally has little effect on the resin; placed after, the resin life is better but the cost and downtime of sanitization must be accepted.

questions.question: Chapter 5 describes the design trend for purified water systems over the last decade. Which statement is correct?

options.A: More than 90% of new systems use single-pass RO as the main treatment, followed by CEDI, ion exchange or a second RO pass
options.B: Ion exchange systems are still the mainstream for new systems, with RO used only for WFI and mostly in two-pass designs
options.C: New systems mostly make Purified Water by distillation, with a multiple-effect still as pretreatment
options.D: New systems no longer use any ion exchange or CEDI, and fully replace them with two-pass RO, omitting the final polishing

questions.explanation: The guide notes a shift from ion exchange systems to membrane systems, mainly because of reduced chemical consumption, ability to reject contaminants, less maintenance, stable operation and lifecycle cost.

questions.question: How do CEDI and conventional ion exchange (IX) differ in how the resin is regenerated?

options.A: CEDI uses an electric field to split water into H+ and OH- to regenerate the resin continuously; IX is regenerated with acid and caustic solutions
options.B: CEDI and IX are the same, both needing periodic batch regeneration with acid and caustic, differing only in equipment size
options.C: CEDI is regenerated with brine and IX with an electric field, with similar regeneration frequency and neither using chemicals
options.D: CEDI needs no regeneration at all, because its media never saturate, and does not need a concentrate stream

questions.explanation: CEDI is a continuous process in which ionized species are drawn into the concentrate stream while the high voltage gradient splits water to regenerate the media continuously, eliminating chemical handling and external regeneration services; a concentrate stream is still always required.

questions.question: According to Section 5.3.2, how does the position of a CEDI unit differ between Purified Water and WFI processes?

options.A: Purified Water: placed before the RO to protect the membrane; WFI: placed after the RO as polishing
options.B: Purified Water or non-compendial water: placed after the RO; USP WFI: placed before the RO
options.C: Both placed before the RO, as pretreatment to reduce the scaling load on the membrane and protect the downstream resin beds
options.D: Both placed after the RO, as the final treatment to ensure stable product water conductivity and lower TOC

questions.explanation: The guide explains that CEDI can be used downstream of RO to make Purified Water, but in a WFI process it is used upstream of the RO, because RO or distillation must serve as the final treatment step for WFI.

questions.question: A plant uses single-pass RO to make Purified Water and finds the product water conductivity too high. According to Section 5.4.3, what is the most likely cause?

options.A: The RO membrane rejects a large amount of carbon dioxide, lowering the product water pH and raising conductivity, and affecting the TOC reading
options.B: Carbon dioxide passes directly through the RO membrane and may push product water conductivity beyond the USP Stage 1 limit
options.C: RO has nearly 100% removal capability for very low molecular weight organics, so conductivity is unaffected
options.D: RO produces no concentrate stream, so salts accumulate on the product side and raise conductivity

questions.explanation: RO cannot remove 100% of contaminants and has little or no removal of CO2 and very small molecular weight organics; single-pass RO typically removes 90-99% of salts and so on, and further purification is generally still needed to meet USP requirements, with two-pass RO being able to comply.

questions.question: A plant uses DI tanks regenerated by an outside service company. Which statement about quality responsibility is correct?

options.A: Responsibility passes entirely to the regeneration service company, and the manufacturer need not exercise control
options.B: As long as the service company holds an ISO certificate, the manufacturer is exempt from quality control
options.C: The manufacturer is responsible only for product water conductivity and not for the condition of the resin
options.D: Outsourcing regeneration does not relieve the manufacturer of quality control responsibility for its ion exchange system

questions.explanation: The note to Table 5-1 states that off-site regeneration does not lessen the manufacturer's responsibility; other drawbacks include loss of control over the use, handling and maintenance of DI tanks, and the fact that DI tanks are an excellent place for microbial growth between regenerations.

questions.question: According to Section 6.2, which statement about the methods permitted for WFI production under US USP and European regulations is correct?

options.A: USP allows only distillation; European regulations allow both distillation and RO, with RO placed after the distillation
options.B: Both USP and European regulations allow only distillation and RO, subject to their respective monograph requirements
options.C: USP allows distillation, RO and UF; European regulations allow only distillation and RO
options.D: USP allows distillation or RO, which must be the final step; European regulations currently allow distillation only

questions.explanation: Section 6.2 states that USP allows WFI to be purified by distillation or RO (which should be the last step), while current European regulations allow distillation only. UF cannot by regulation be used to produce compendial WFI (see Section 2.5), so the statement that USP allows distillation, RO and UF is wrong.

questions.question: How does a still achieve endotoxin removal, and how much endotoxin reduction can generally be provided?

options.A: After the water evaporates, a separator removes entrained droplets (containing endotoxin), providing at least a 3 log10 reduction
options.B: High temperature destroys endotoxin completely, so a 6 log10 reduction can be guaranteed, with no separator and no monitoring needed
options.C: Ion exchange resin adsorbs endotoxin, reducing it by about 1 log10, and the resin needs periodic regeneration
options.D: The condenser filters out endotoxin directly, with no separator needed, providing about a 2 log10 reduction

questions.explanation: Distillation relies on the phase change and separation of entrainment; the separator removes fine mist and entrained impurities, including endotoxin; the reduction is at least 3 log10 (99.99%), and the specific load limit should still be confirmed with the manufacturer.

questions.topic: Pretreatment for ME vs VC stills
questions.question: A plant's feed water has only been softened and dechlorinated, and it must choose a still. According to Section 6.5.5, which is more suitable?

options.A: A VC still, because basic pretreatment needs only softening, dechlorination and ammonia removal; an ME still needs very low TDS and low silica
options.B: An ME still, because its high operating pressure means it has the lowest feed water quality requirements and needs no softening
options.C: Either one, because the pretreatment requirements are the same for all stills regardless of type
options.D: A VC still, but the water must first pass through RO and CEDI to reduce TDS to below 10 mg/L

questions.explanation: An ME still operates at higher pressure and temperature and needs higher quality feed water (TDS preferably below 10 mg/L and silica below 1 mg/L), usually with ion exchange or RO pretreatment; the basic VC requirements are softening, dechlorination and removal of volatiles.

questions.question: RO is acceptable for producing WFI, but what needs special attention when it is used?

options.A: RO permeate is too hot and must be cooled before storage, otherwise it will damage the inner surface of the storage tank
options.B: RO permeate is cold and lacks the microbial protection of distillation's high temperature; and membrane or seal failure will contaminate the product water
options.C: RO has insufficient endotoxin removal capability, so it must never be used for WFI, with or without post-treatment
options.D: RO permeate carries no microbial risk, because the membrane pore size is fixed, and no additional sanitization is needed

questions.explanation: RO permeate is cold, so it lacks the temperature protection of distillation; membrane or seal failure contaminates the product water directly, and this must be controlled through pretreatment, membrane material selection, integrity challenges, periodic sanitization and monitoring.

questions.question: Comparing single-effect (SE) and multiple-effect (ME) stills, which statement is correct?

options.A: Because of multiple distillations, ME water quality is clearly better than SE, and its endotoxin removal capability is also stronger
options.B: SE has lower operating cost, so SE is still the mainstay for large WFI demand, with ME limited to small quantities
options.C: The more effects an ME has, the lower the capital cost, but the higher the steam and cooling water consumption
options.D: Water quality is equivalent (the water is distilled only once in both); the advantage of ME is much lower utility cost

questions.explanation: In both SE and ME the water is distilled only once, so quality is equal; ME uses pure steam from each effect to heat the next, so steam and cooling water use is low. As the number of effects increases, capital cost rises and steam and cooling water consumption falls. Large demand is met by ME or VC in place of SE.

questions.question: What is the main difference between utility steam and clean steam?

options.A: Utility steam is generated from treated water with no additives; clean steam comes from the utility boiler and contains pH buffers and corrosion inhibitors, and requires daily testing
options.B: Utility steam comes from the utility boiler, often contains anti-scaling and anti-corrosion additives, and has a higher pH; clean steam is generated from treated water and contains no amines
options.C: The two have the same source, except that clean steam is additionally 0.2 μm filtered and has condensate recovery
options.D: The condensate of clean steam has a higher pH because it contains amine buffering substances and corrosion-inhibiting additives

questions.explanation: To protect boilers and piping, utility steam often has additives such as amines, with a pH of about 9.5-10.5; filtration removes only particles and cannot remove dissolved substances such as amines. Clean steam has no additives, its condensate is unbuffered, and its pH is relatively lower.

questions.question: Which statement about regulatory requirements for clean steam is correct?

options.A: USP has a clean steam monograph that sets an endotoxin limit, a condensate pH range and a sampling frequency
options.B: The FDA requires clean steam condensate to meet the WFI specification, with batch-by-batch release testing
options.C: Neither the FDA nor USP has minimum standards for clean steam; but the LVP cGMP requires that boiler feed water for steam contacting product contain no amines or hydrazine
options.D: 21 CFR requires clean steam generators to use 316L stainless steel, with annual repassivation and FDA inspection

questions.explanation: The guide states that there is no FDA or USP minimum standard for clean steam, and no regulation specifying material, instrumentation or surface finish. Users are responsible for the suitability of their own steam, which is why practices vary widely and are often over-conservative.

questions.question: A facility needs steam only for heating, yet installs a clean steam generator. According to Section 7.1, what kind of problem is this?

options.A: A necessary regulatory requirement, because any steam that touches the process area needs clean steam
options.B: Reasonable risk management, because clean steam lowers cost and improves system reliability
options.C: Inappropriate, because a clean steam generator cannot be used for heating and would damage the equipment
options.D: Over-conservatism; where a simple pressure reducing station would do, it instead adds equipment, cost and complexity and affects reliability

questions.explanation: The guide's example: when utility steam is sufficient to maintain product quality, installing a clean steam generator instead of a simple steam reducing station adds equipment and cost and lowers reliability; over-specifying pretreatment or using WFI as feed water are similar cases.

questions.question: When the steam pressure differential of a clean steam generator greatly exceeds the design condition, what is the main risk and the recommended countermeasure?

options.A: Steam velocity that is too low causes condensate to accumulate; increase the steam differential pressure and raise the feed water temperature
options.B: Steam velocity in the separator that is too high may carry over endotoxin; set an alarm and shut the unit down
options.C: The condensate pH rises; add acid automatically and increase sampling frequency and number
options.D: The feed pump is overloaded; lower the supply steam temperature and shorten the equipment's running time

questions.explanation: The entrainment separator works within an optimal velocity range, and a large increase in steam flow causes endotoxin carryover. Feed level control likewise uses a high-level alarm and shutdown to prevent flooding of the evaporator and carryover.

questions.question: In steam sampling, how do steam "quality" and "purity" differ in meaning?

options.A: Quality refers to the chemical purity and endotoxin of the steam; purity refers to the degree of saturation and dryness of the steam
options.B: They mean the same, with only different terms used by different regulations and countries, and no real difference
options.C: Quality refers to saturation (measuring dryness and non-condensable gases); purity is tested on the condensate, such as conductivity and endotoxin
options.D: Quality has a minimum value set by the FDA; purity has a minimum value set by EN 285

questions.explanation: In the guide, quality is the saturation of the steam; the FDA and USP have no minimum steam quality requirement, and criteria exist only in European EN 285. Purity depends on the product, process and use, commonly assessed with a sample cooler and conductivity meter, and sampling at the point of use is recommended.

questions.topic: Role and drawback of storage tanks
questions.question: According to Section 8.2.1, what is the function and the drawback of a storage tank in a water system?

options.A: It can eliminate microbial risk; the drawback is only that it increases capital cost and takes up plant space
options.B: It can replace the distribution loop; the drawback is that it cannot provide reserve capacity or buffer peak demand
options.C: It can absorb peak demand, letting the generation system be smaller and run continuously; the drawbacks are added cost and slow-flow zones that may encourage bacteria
options.D: It allows the system to be larger and lowers microbial risk; the drawback is that UF is needed to remove endotoxin, with more energy, before release

questions.explanation: Storage lets a smaller, cheaper generation system meet peak demand, and its cost is usually lower than oversizing pretreatment equipment for peaks; but a tank also introduces slow-velocity zones, so designs include spray balls, vent filters and so on.

questions.question: Comparing the batch and dynamic/continuous distribution concepts, which statement is correct?

options.A: Batch uses a single tank for continuous supply; dynamic requires at least two tanks alternating for test and release, at higher cost
options.B: Both require testing before release, except that batch has shorter storage time and needs smaller tanks, with the same lifecycle cost
options.C: The advantage of dynamic is that every batch can be QA released, but lifecycle cost is higher
options.D: Batch uses at least two tanks, alternating supply and fill-test-release; dynamic uses a single tank for continuous supply

questions.explanation: The advantage of batch is that water is tested and QA released before use, but capital and operating costs are high and operation is cumbersome, so it is generally used for small systems; dynamic piping is simpler and operation more efficient. The guide also notes that on-line conductivity and TOC can provide similar assurance at lower cost.

questions.question: A plant uses a hot storage, hot distribution (>65°C) system and finds the hydrophobic vent filter on the tank often wetted by moisture. According to Section 8.3.4, what is a reasonable countermeasure?

options.A: Switch to a larger pore size filter so moisture passes through more easily, lowering filter differential pressure and reducing change frequency
options.B: Stop using the vent filter and vent the tank directly to atmosphere, to avoid the filter being wetted
options.C: Position the filter so that it drains well, and heat it with a low-pressure steam jacket or electric heat tracing to prevent condensation
options.D: Lower the system temperature to below 30°C, to avoid moisture and reduce the filter change frequency

questions.explanation: Concerns for hot systems include preventing personnel scalding, circulation pump cavitation (NPSH must account for hot water vapor pressure), moisture condensation in vent filters, and rouge formation. Heating the filter prevents condensation; removing the filter loses protection against microorganisms and particles.

questions.question: What is the guide's position on deadleg length?

options.A: It adopts 6D as a mandatory regulatory limit, measured from the outside of the pipe wall, and anything beyond is regarded as a violation
options.B: It recommends measuring from the outside pipe wall while avoiding a hard maximum; water quality must still be met, and deadlegs should be kept as short as possible
options.C: It adopts 3D as an FDA requirement, measured from the main centerline, with no exceptions and no risk assessment needed
options.D: As long as zero-deadleg valves are used, length need not be considered, and no sampling confirmation is needed

questions.explanation: 6D comes from the 1976 draft CFR 212 and is measured from the centerline of the main, while 3D is measured from the outside wall of the pipe; the different measurement bases are easily confused. The guide recommends measuring from the outside wall but sets no hard rule; the point is that water quality meets requirements and deadlegs are minimized.

questions.question: According to common industry practice, what are the minimum return velocity and flow regime requirements for a circulation loop?

options.A: A minimum of 1 ft/s, with Reynolds number below 2,100 to maintain laminar flow, to avoid biofilm shedding and contamination caused by shear
options.B: A minimum return velocity of 3 ft/s or more and turbulent flow with Reynolds number above 2,100; hot, cold or ozonated loops may be slightly lower
options.C: A minimum of 3 ft/s that must never be lower under any circumstances, including shutdown and heat-up periods
options.D: A minimum of 10 ft/s, with Reynolds number above 10,000, to prevent biofilm formation

questions.explanation: A common design is a return velocity of at least 3 ft/s and turbulent flow (Re > 2,100), providing shear to hinder biofilm attachment. Systems less favorable to microbial growth, such as hot, cold or ozonated ones, can accept a lower velocity for short periods; the loop must still be kept full and under positive pressure.

questions.question: How does this guide describe on-line monitoring of water quality?

options.A: No pharmacopoeia or regulation requires on-line monitoring; a monitoring plan may combine on-line instruments, manual records and laboratory analysis
options.B: USP requires all Purified Water and WFI systems to monitor conductivity and TOC on-line
options.C: The FDA requires on-line monitoring only when WFI is used
options.D: Laboratory analysis is not accepted, and everything must be changed to on-line

questions.explanation: Section 9 notes that many quality attributes can be monitored continuously, but no pharmacopoeia or regulation requires on-line monitoring; the optimum degree of automation must balance better process control, documentation and labor cost against the cost of instrument purchase, qualification and maintenance.

questions.question: A water system controls microorganisms by final product water temperature. According to Chapter 9, which set of judgments is correct?

options.A: Both the product water temperature and the heating steam temperature must be regarded as critical, and both must be qualified, calibrated and reconfirmed every quarter
options.B: Both need only be commissioned per GEP, with no qualification and no calibration
options.C: The product water temperature sensor and alarm are critical and need qualification; the heating medium (such as steam) temperature does not
options.D: Product water temperature is not critical, because temperature is not a water quality attribute and is only a general process parameter

questions.explanation: Instruments and control systems used to measure, monitor, control or record a critical process parameter are critical and require qualification; the guide also recommends marking them in documents and identifying non-critical instruments on the field devices.

questions.question: A plant wants to use an on-line conductivity meter for the final QA release test of Purified Water. Which practice is correct?

options.A: Use uncompensated conductivity and measure water temperature at the same time, because errors in temperature compensation algorithms make compensated values unsuitable for critical QA tests
options.B: Use a value temperature-compensated to 25°C, because compensation improves accuracy and simplifies interpretation
options.C: Measure only conductivity and do not record temperature, because the instrument corrects for temperature automatically
options.D: On-line conductivity cannot be used for the final QA test and must be measured off-line in a laboratory to be accepted, completed within 24 hours

questions.explanation: On-line conductivity can be used for the final QA test without periodic laboratory analysis, but per USP the uncompensated conductivity and the water temperature must be measured; compensated values are for process control and monitoring only and are not bound by USP requirements.

questions.question: Someone proposes replacing the endotoxin test with TOC trending. According to this guide, which statement is correct?

options.A: TOC and endotoxin have a clear quantitative conversion, so TOC results can replace the endotoxin test
options.B: TOC detects only inorganic contamination and so has nothing to do with endotoxin, and the two cannot be cross-referenced
options.C: Endotoxin contamination raises TOC, but the two are not quantitatively correlated, and TOC cannot replace the endotoxin test
options.D: As long as TOC is below 500 ppb, the endotoxin and microbial tests can be omitted, with annual confirmation

questions.explanation: TOC is a total indicator of organic carbon in water, with a nominal USP limit of 500 ppb; endotoxin contamination brings higher TOC, but there is no quantitative relationship, so TOC cannot replace microbial or endotoxin testing.

questions.question: A plant uses ozone to control microorganisms and wants to use an ORP analyzer to control ozone concentration. According to the guide, which statement is correct?

options.A: It can be used, because ORP is specific to ozone and responds quickly, suiting continuous monitoring
options.B: It can be used, but must be calibrated daily with buffer solution and used with temperature compensation
options.C: It should not be used; ORP analyzers are non-specific and cannot distinguish ozone from other oxidants
options.D: It should not be used, because ORP values are affected by conductivity and cannot be measured, and cannot be read on-line

questions.explanation: The guide recommends monitoring dissolved ozone at the tank outlet, downstream of the UV and in the loop return, using wet chemistry periodically or an on-line analyzer continuously; ORP cannot tell ozone from other oxidants and should not be used to control ozone.

questions.question: According to Chapter 10, what are the purpose and approach of the first phase of a water system sampling plan?

options.A: To demonstrate that the system complies over the long term; sampling each use point once a quarter is enough, with no daily monitoring
options.B: To test only whether the feed water meets drinking water standards, with no sampling of other treatment steps or use points
options.C: To end once SOPs are established, with no review of records or establishment of failure investigation procedures and sanitization data, and no confirmatory sampling
options.D: To establish operating ranges and provide the basis for cleaning and sanitization procedures; sampling after each step and at each use point daily for two to four weeks

questions.explanation: The first phase includes sampling of the feed water, each treatment step and the use points, and ends with completed operating and maintenance SOPs and a process for determining, when verification fails, whether the problem is local or systemic.

questions.question: In the second phase, a plant finds that rarely used use points are sampled and flushed every day. What is the problem with this practice?

options.A: Routinely flushing seldom-used points can mask early signs of local microbial growth; sampling each point at least weekly is recommended
options.B: Sampling frequency is insufficient, because in phase two every use point must be sampled daily with no flushing, to ensure representativeness
options.C: There is no problem; frequent sampling only adds data and makes trend analysis more accurate
options.D: It should change to monthly sampling, to avoid interfering with the process and to lower the contamination risk from sampling

questions.explanation: The second phase is to show that the system, when operated per SOP, continues to deliver water within the predetermined range. The guide recommends sampling each point at least weekly and warns that overly frequent sampling of seldom-used points masks local contamination through artificial flushing.

questions.question: What are the purpose and duration of the third phase of the sampling plan?

options.A: To demonstrate the system's microbial limits, usually 30 consecutive days, sampling each use point daily
options.B: To establish alert and action limits, usually two consecutive weeks, sampling after each treatment step with trend analysis
options.C: To demonstrate that the system continues to supply acceptable water over the long term (usually one year), covering seasonal variation in feed water
options.D: To verify instrument calibration and the accuracy of on-line sensors, usually one quarter, with laboratory comparison

questions.explanation: The third phase uses the established procedures; for WFI systems, FDA guidance recommends sampling at least one use point daily and testing all use points weekly. After a full year of testing, validation is considered complete, and continued monitoring then builds the record.

questions.question: Which statement about the particular points Chapter 10 makes on water system documentation is correct?

options.A: Only P&IDs are needed, with no field test reports and no supplementary isometric drawings
options.B: The system specification need only list design parameters, with no performance standards or corresponding acceptance criteria
options.C: Qualification results need only be pass or fail, with no comparison to acceptance criteria or recording of measured values, and no sign-off
options.D: Isometric drawings with weld numbers, elevations, slopes and drain points can be added; field inspection reports cover passivation, welding, slope and deadleg-free records

questions.explanation: The text requires the specification to list both performance standards and design parameters, and test results to be compared directly with acceptance criteria set according to the system design and operating specification; qualification testing should also include automated functions, temperature control, distribution flow velocity and initial water quality determination.

questions.topic: Use of water during sampling phases
questions.question: Can the water produced during the phases of the sampling plan be used for manufacturing?

options.A: No; the full year of sampling must be finished before use, with bottled water substituted in the meantime
options.B: Yes, with no conditions, because sampling is only monitoring and does not affect product release decisions, and no QA approval is needed
options.C: Yes, provided the analytical results are acceptable; before use, consider whether the amount of data is sufficient given the intended use and the effect of water quality
options.D: It may be used only for cleaning and not for product preparation, with residues separately confirmed after cleaning

questions.explanation: The guide states that the first sampling phase begins after the system has been shown fully operational through integrated OQ testing, and the water produced during it may be used in manufacturing as long as analytical results are acceptable, though how much data is needed depends on the intended use and the effect of water quality.

questions.question: In the USP three-stage conductivity test, what does Stage 1 require?

options.A: Measure pH in the laboratory and raise the ionic strength with saturated KCl solution before judging conductivity, performed daily
options.B: Mainly an in-line test, measuring conductivity and water temperature at the same time with an uncompensated sensor
options.C: Heat the sample to 100°C before measuring conductivity, and compare with the room temperature measurement to judge
options.D: Judge by the temperature-compensated conductivity value, with no need to record temperature and no off-line sampling

questions.explanation: Stage 1 is an in-line test; failing it leads to Stage 2 (off-line sampling, adjusting temperature and stirring, then comparing with the table value), and failing that leads to the Stage 3 laboratory test, which requires pH measurement. In Stage 3, saturated KCl is used to raise the ionic strength.

questions.question: Which statement about USP requirements for TOC instruments is correct?

options.A: Only specific brands of instrument may be used and all others are unacceptable, with USP certification and return to the manufacturer for calibration every quarter
options.B: It must measure organic and inorganic carbon combined, with a detection limit of 5 mg/L, with no need to distinguish the source or demonstrate suitability, with calibration once a year
options.C: It must completely oxidize organics to CO2 and discriminate inorganic carbon, have a detection limit of 0.05 mg/L or lower, and have its suitability demonstrated periodically
options.D: No suitability demonstration is needed, only annual calibration, and no system suitability test

questions.explanation: USP does not restrict the technology, only the functions the instrument must have; in-line testing may be standardized once per operating day, and the frequency of suitability tests can range from every off-line test to once a month.

questions.question: Comparing EP and USP requirements for water, which statement is correct?

options.A: EP allows only distillation to make WFI, and source water need only have its history recorded; USP requires source water to meet drinking water standards
options.B: EP allows RO to make WFI; USP allows only distillation, and source water must meet drinking water standards
options.C: EP has adopted the TOC test and dropped the pH test, while USP still uses the wet-chemistry oxidizable substances test and the pH test
options.D: The two have exactly the same sample volume requirements for WFI, and the same requirements for source water

questions.explanation: EP requires a sample volume of 100 mL for Purified Water and 500 mL for WFI, does not include TOC, and retains a separate pH test; European inspectors also pay particular attention to the drainability of the system through the use points.

questions.question: Which statement about European specifications for sterilizing steam is correct?

options.A: EP has a clean steam monograph and requires endotoxin of no more than 0.25 EU per mL and a conductivity limit
options.B: EN 285 regulates only water conductivity and has no requirements for steam dryness and non-condensable gases
options.C: EP does not regulate clean steam; sterilizing steam quality is governed by EN 285, with a dryness value of 0.9 or more (0.95 for metal loads)
options.D: Europe has no steam quality specification at all; each plant sets its own and files it with the authority, with no separate verification needed

questions.explanation: EP is the pharmacopoeial source for water standards but does not regulate clean steam; the UK additionally has HTM-2010 and HTM-2031. Superheated steam sterilizes poorly, and non-condensable gases (NCG) can form air pockets that impede steam penetration.

questions.question: What is the order of the four main steps of stainless steel passivation?

options.A: Acid wash, then water rinse, then solvent degreasing, then final water rinse until the outlet conductivity is acceptable
options.B: Solvent degreasing, then water rinse, then acid wash (passivation), then final water rinse until the outlet quality is comparable
options.C: Water rinse, then acid wash, then final water rinse, then solvent degreasing, and finally nitrogen drying and sealing
options.D: Solvent degreasing, then acid wash, then drying, then final water rinse until the outlet quality matches the inlet

questions.explanation: The purpose of passivation is to maximize the corrosion resistance of stainless steel: grease is removed first, then rinsed, an acid wash removes free iron and oxides, and a final rinse follows; the Cr/Fe atomic ratio of the oxide film should be at least 1:1, with 2:1 or higher ideal (Section 11.3.3).

questions.question: How is water softener resin regenerated?

options.A: By alternately flushing the resin with sulfuric acid and sodium hydroxide, producing H+ and OH- to replace the hardness ions
options.B: By passing concentrated sodium chloride brine through the resin, so that the hardness ions (calcium, magnesium) are replaced by sodium ions
options.C: By applying electricity to split water and regenerate the resin continuously, with no regeneration chemicals used
options.D: By flushing the resin with 80°C hot water so that calcium and magnesium ions are thermally desorbed and carried out in the drain

questions.explanation: The resin has a higher affinity for multivalent ions than for sodium, so concentrated brine is needed to overcome this affinity and complete regeneration. Softeners are the industry standard and low in cost, but salt and spent brine must be handled.

questions.question: When acidification and degasification are used as an alternative to a softener, what operating conditions does the text describe?

options.A: Sulfuric acid adjusts the feed water to a pH of about 3.8-4.2, followed by degasification in a packed tower; before the RO it is adjusted back to about 8.0-8.5
options.B: Hydrochloric acid adjusts to a pH of about 10-11, converting carbon dioxide to carbonate, followed by degasification in a packed tower, with no adjustment before the RO
options.C: Sulfuric acid adjusts to a pH of about 6.5-7.0, and before the RO it is adjusted to 3.8-4.2 to aid membrane desalting efficiency
options.D: No pH adjustment is needed; air aeration alone removes CO2, with no further adjustment before the RO

questions.explanation: After acidification to about 3.8-4.2, free CO2 is stripped with air in a packed tower at better than 98% efficiency, and the pH after degasification is about 6.5-7.0. The advantage is avoiding the handling of large amounts of salt, and sulfate is more easily removed by RO than sodium; the drawbacks are acid handling and two pH adjustments.

questions.question: A plant's still feed water is changed from deionized water to softened water. According to Section 11.6.2, how will the recovery ratio change?

options.A: It rises; softened water contains sodium salts, which raise evaporation efficiency and reduce concentrated blowdown, increasing recovery by about 5-10%
options.B: It is unchanged; recovery depends only on the number of effects of the still, regardless of feed water quality and TDS, and is not affected by pretreatment
options.C: It falls; recovery with deionized feed can reach 90-95% and with softened water is usually 80-85%, because the higher the TDS, the lower it is
options.D: It rises to 95-99%, because the hardness of softened water has been removed and the scaling risk is greatly reduced

questions.explanation: Part of the feed must be blown down continuously to limit TDS in the evaporator. Rc = Md/Mf and Mf = Md + Mb, limited by the scale-forming potential; the higher the feed TDS, the lower the recovery ratio.

questions.topic: Number of effects in ME still
questions.question: What results from increasing the number of effects in a multiple-effect (ME) still?

options.A: Product output rises markedly, but steam and cooling water use also rise, and capital cost increases
options.B: Output does not increase, but the steam and cooling water needed to produce the same amount of distillate are reduced
options.C: Distillate quality improves, because the water is distilled more times, and endotoxin removal is also higher
options.D: The more effects the better, with no cost limit, and more effects make operation simpler

questions.explanation: The number of effects is limited by the temperature range and equipment cost, and the fixed cost of additional effects eventually offsets the energy savings; a typical ME has 3-5 effects, and some have up to 8. The larger the system output and the more expensive the steam, the more reasonable it is to add effects.

questions.question: What are the consequences if non-condensable gases (CO2, oxygen) in a still are not properly vented?

options.A: They only lower the distillate pH, without affecting heat transfer efficiency or the stainless steel surface
options.B: They blanket the heat transfer surface, lowering output, and being corrosive cause pitting, embrittlement and cracking of the stainless steel
options.C: They increase still output, because the gases assist heat transfer and reduce condenser load and cooling water use
options.D: They cause problems only in vacuum-operated stills, with pressurized stills unaffected

questions.explanation: Non-condensable gases are released as water temperature rises and, being heavy, collect at the bottom and tend to move to the coldest surface; the still vent should always show a steady stream of steam. Poor venting or failed distillate level control may carry CO2 into the pump suction and cause high conductivity.

questions.topic: Clean steam generator at lower pressure
questions.question: A clean steam generator designed to produce 2000 lbs/hr at 60 psig is operated at 30 psig. According to the Section 11.7 calculation, what is the result?

options.A: Output falls to about 50%, steam velocity is unchanged, so separator performance and water quality are unaffected, and alarm settings need no adjustment
options.B: Output is about unchanged, only the temperature falls, and separator velocity and endotoxin removal are not affected, with no need for reconfirmation
options.C: Output rises to about 3,665 lbs/hr (about 183%), steam velocity rises about 300%, and contaminants risk being carried over through the separator
options.D: Output rises about 183%, but separator velocity is unaffected, so there is no risk of contaminant carryover

questions.explanation: Steam generation is proportional to the temperature difference between the supply steam and the clean steam; the difference rises from 39.67°F to 72.7°F. The steam volume rises about 296% while the separator passage area is unchanged, so velocity increases; an excessive temperature difference may also cause a "dry wall" effect and leave scale.

questions.question: When planning plant steam supply for a clean steam generator, what flow allowance does the text recommend?

options.A: Reserve the same as the clean steam output (100%), with no additional margin and no consideration of a feed water heater
options.B: Reserve 200% or more, to ensure sufficient pressure differential and avoid insufficient steam velocity
options.C: Reserve 110-120% of the maximum expected output; close to 110% with a feed water heater and low TDS, and close to 120% without a heater
options.D: Reserve 50-60%, because plant steam only supplies preheating, with the remaining heat made up by electric heaters

questions.explanation: The text also notes that plant steam pressure should be nominally 50-60 psig higher than clean steam pressure; feed water flow is about 105-110% of output at very low TDS and 115-120% at higher TDS.

questions.question: Bacillus is detected in a plant's water sample. According to the text, what is the most likely source of contamination?

options.A: Improper handling by the sampler, such as not wearing gloves (Bacillus is typical of sample handling problems)
options.B: Water-borne contamination of the water system itself (typically Gram-negative rods such as Pseudomonas)
options.C: Excess chlorine in the feed water causing bacteria to clump and form biofilm on the pipe wall
options.D: Environmental contamination at the sampling point (Bacillus is common in the environment of sample ports)

questions.explanation: The text indicates that Staphylococcus typically represents a sample handling problem, Bacillus represents environmental contamination of the sample port, and Gram-negative rods are typical of water-borne contamination. Identifying the microorganism provides strong evidence of the contamination source.

questions.question: According to the text, which statement about operating temperature and risk in hot water systems is correct?

options.A: Circulating water kept at 40-50°C is self-sanitizing, with no separate hot sanitization and no periodic monitoring needed
options.B: The higher the temperature the better; above 90°C rouge is eliminated completely and the life of the stainless steel is extended
options.C: With circulating water kept at 75-85°C, the system can return to use after shutdown and maintenance without sanitization
options.D: Circulation at 75-85°C is generally regarded as self-sanitizing; above 87°C rouge is easily produced, and 96°C outlet water may cause pump cavitation

questions.explanation: After maintenance or shutdown the system must still be sanitized: flush the system, sample points and use points with 80°C hot water, with a flush of two to three times the volume of the distribution system sufficing; heated systems are typically designed to heat water from 15°C to 80°C in two to four hours.

questions.question: Why does the text recommend purchasing 316L fittings, valves and tubing of the same pipe size with the same Heat Number as far as possible?

options.A: Because the Heat Number determines the corrosion resistance grade of the stainless steel, and materials with different numbers cannot be mixed
options.B: Because each heat of steel differs in composition, so melting point and the required welding current differ; the same Heat Number gives consistent welding parameters
options.C: Because the same Heat Number eliminates passivation and saves time on subsequent acid washing and rinsing
options.D: Because the higher the Heat Number, the lower the sulfur content, so weldability and corrosion resistance are better, and post-weld inspection is also eliminated

questions.explanation: The allowable variation in chromium, molybdenum, nickel and carbon in 316L is large and affects melting point and welding machine current; the text also notes that inconsistent sulfur content in mating parts has adverse effects that outweigh the benefit of low sulfur, with a recommended compromise sulfur range of 0.005%-0.02%.

questions.question: According to Section 11.10, which statement about distribution piping design requirements is correct?

options.A: Minimum slope of 1/16 in./ft; sanitary diaphragm valves installed at about 60 degrees from vertical to aid drainage; tri-clamp connections
options.B: Minimum slope of 1 in./ft; ball valves installed horizontally, with welded or flanged joints and no further consideration of drainage
options.C: No slope at all, as long as circulation is maintained, with butterfly valves as the main isolation valves and threaded joints
options.D: Butterfly valves with threaded joints, with the threads sealed using PTFE tape

questions.explanation: The guide requires natural drainage and verified slope (checked externally after hanging and before insulation), and PTFE is preferred as the diaphragm face material for valves. The purpose of slope and drainage design is to avoid water remaining in the system.

questions.question: Before orbital welding of stainless steel pipe, what is required of the argon purge gas?

options.A: 99.999% purity, with water content below 1 ppm or oxygen below 2 ppm, and air completely purged before welding
options.B: 95% purity is enough, with only a small flow during welding and no need to purge the air from the pipe beforehand
options.C: 99.999% purity, but air may be purged slowly after welding starts, to save gas and shorten preparation time
options.D: 99% purity, with water content below 100 ppm, and only a brief purge of air from the pipe before welding

questions.explanation: Orbital welding is an autogenous TIG process (no filler material), requires inert gas shielding, and the air in the pipe must be completely purged before welding. Many weld defects (such as lack of internal purge gas, interrupted purge gas and poor purity; Sections 11.11.7.5-11.11.7.8) are related to the purge gas.

questions.question: QC finds a weld that does not pass. According to Section 11.11.9, how should it be handled?

options.A: Repair weld in place with the same parameters, recording the number of repairs and the welder, then reinspect
options.B: It must not be rewelded or repaired; cut out the rejected weld, dress the pipe ends and weld again
options.C: Use manual repair welding to correct internal wall depressions, then reinspect the weld bead with a borescope
options.D: Accept the weld, but increase the sampling frequency in that area and mark its location on the piping drawing

questions.explanation: The text states plainly that "Rewelding or weld repairs are not acceptable". The remedy is to saw out the weld, keep the cut-out section where possible for further examination, check that discoloration and the heat-affected zone are completely removed, then dress and deburr the pipe ends with dedicated equipment and reweld.

questions.question: If the action limit for Purified Water is 100 CFU/mL and for WFI is 10 CFU/100 mL, about how many times stricter is the WFI microbial limit than that of Purified Water?

options.A: About 10 times, because the units of the two limits are the same and the values can simply be divided, with no conversion of volume basis needed
options.B: About 100 times, because the Purified Water limit value is 100 times the WFI limit value, with the same units
options.C: About 10,000 times (Purified Water 100 CFU/mL against WFI 10 CFU/100 mL)
options.D: About 1,000 times (Purified Water about 10,000 CFU/100 mL against WFI 10 CFU/100 mL)

questions.explanation: Putting the units on a per 100 mL basis, 100 CFU/mL equals 10,000 CFU/100 mL, against 10 CFU/100 mL for WFI, a 1,000-fold difference. WFI also has an explicit endotoxin limit requirement.

questions.question: In the clean preparation area for welded piping, how should cleaned pipe that will not be welded within two hours be handled?

options.A: Cover the pipe ends or the whole pipe with clear plastic bags and tape them securely, to prevent contamination
options.B: Place it on shelves in the general workshop, then rinse with water and visually inspect before use
options.C: Cover only with a lint-free cloth, without bagging, and store on stainless steel racks
options.D: Seal the pipe ends directly with ordinary tape and store on carbon steel racks, with no need to clean again before use

questions.explanation: The text requires pipe ends to be cleaned with isopropyl alcohol (IPA) and lint-free wipes and not touched with bare hands; fittings should also remain in sealed bags until welding. The clean area should not be used for equipment that has processed carbon steel, and personnel wear shoe covers and lint-free gloves.
